title: Rate dependent effects of acute nicotine on risk taking in young ...
abstract:
## Abstract

Beneficial effects of nicotine on cognition and behavioral control are hypothesized to relate to the high rates of cigarette smoking in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Given that ADHD is associated with both impulsivity and elevated risk taking, we hypothesized that nicotine modulates risk taking, as it does impulsivity. 26 non-smoking young adults (15 controls with normal impulsivity and 11 ADHD with high impulsivity) received 7 mg transdermal nicotine, 20 mg oral mecamylamine, and placebo on separate days, followed by the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART).
Statistical analyses found no group differences in baseline risk taking. Reexamination of the data using a median split on baseline risk taking, to create high (HRT) and low (LRT) risk taking groups, revealed significant effects of nicotinic drugs that differed by group. Nicotine reduced risk taking in HRT and mecamylamine increased risk taking in LRT.
This finding supports the hypothesis that nicotinic receptor function modulates risk taking broadly, beyond those with ADHD, and is consistent with rate dependent cholinergic modulation of other cognitive functions. Further, the results demonstrate that high impulsivity is separable from high risk taking in young adults with ADHD, supporting the utility of these differential behavioral phenotypes for neurobiological studies.
**Keywords:** risk taking, Balloon Analog Risk Task, cholinergic, nicotine, mecamylamine, impulsivity, ADHD, acetylcholine

Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with cognitive deficits on domains including sustained attention (Posner and Dehaene, 1994), working memory (Barkley, 1997), complex organization and planning (Barkley, 1997, Pennington and Ozonoff, 1996), temporal information processing (Barkley, 1997, Barkley *et al.
*, 2001, Zakay, 1992), and most robustly with impulsivity (Willcutt *et al.*, 2005). Specifically, a meta-analysis of cognitive domains affected in ADHD found the largest and most consistent deficits in response inhibition (Willcutt *et al.*, 2005).
Deficits in response inhibition have particular importance as they are related to many functional impairments in ADHD including poor work performance, difficulty forming and maintaining relationships, injuries, alcohol and substance abuse and dependence, and aggression (Barkley *et al.*, 1991, Barkley *et al.*, 1996, Biederman *et al.*, 1991).
Interestingly, adolescents and adults with ADHD initiate cigarette smoking earlier, have significantly higher rates of smoking, and have a more difficult time quitting than a comparable community sample (Kollins
*et al.*, 2005, Milberger *et al.*, 1997, Pomerleau *et al.*, 1995). It has been suggested that individuals with ADHD may use smoking as a form of self-medication to manage difficulties of attention and impulsivity (Levin *et al.*, 1996, Potter *et al.
*, 2006, Wilens *et al.*, 2007). In recent years literature has emerged lending support to this hypothesis, documenting beneficial effects of nicotine and nicotinic agonists on attention, working memory and response inhibition in individuals with ADHD (Wilens *et al.*, 2006). Specific to impulsivity, studies in adolescents and young adults with ADHD have found that acute doses of nicotine improve performance on the Stop Signal Task (SST), a laboratory measure of response inhibition (Potter and Newhouse, 2004, 2008).

Much of the research on nicotine and reward processing has been conducted in cigarette smokers, creating confounds including nicotine addiction and withdrawal processes, and making it difficult to draw conclusions about nicotinic receptor function and reward independent of cigarette smoking. However, it has recently been shown that acute transdermal nicotine enhances the salience of rewarding stimuli in healthy non-smokers (Barr
*et al.*, 2008). The mechanism for this finding may be related to nicotinic receptors in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) which alter neuronal activity to enhance dopamine release and are necessary for the rewarding effects of nicotine (Mansvelder *et al.*, 2003, Nisell *et al.
*, 1994, Schilstrom *et al.*, 1998). Thus, given that deficits in response inhibition are improved with acute nicotine in ADHD (Potter and Newhouse, 2004, 2008) and that nicotine modulates reward salience (Barr *et al.*, 2008, Paterson, 2009), we propose that high risk taking in ADHD may be related to nicotinic cholinergic receptor function.

## 2. Experimental Design and Methods

### 2.1 Overview

While the present risk taking data are novel and have not been published previously, other data from this investigation of the effects of cholinergic manipulation on impulsivity in young adults with and without Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) have been reported in part elsewhere (Potter
*et al.*, 2012). This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of Vermont and was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and all other relevant regulations. This was an acute, single dose, within-subjects, double blind study with three drug conditions: nicotine, mecamylamine, and placebo. After obtaining informed consent, each subject participated in three study days, separated by at least 48 hours, at the General Clinical Research Center (GCRC) of the University of Vermont.

### 2.2 Participants

Subjects were recruited via posters on local college campuses. Fifty nine individuals provided consent and completed a screening visit, of which, 27 non-smoking young adults (18–25 years old) entered the study. The 32 screen fails were due to scheduling conflicts, failure to meet impulsivity criteria, medical contraindication, psychiatric co-morbidity, nicotine use, co-morbid learning disability, recreational use of psychostimulants, and failure to meet ADHD criteria. One subject dropped out of the study for personal reasons resulting in 26 subjects who completed the study.

### 3.2 The Highly Impulsive ADHD Group is not High Risk Taking

There were no significant main effects of group on either AAP [t(24) = 0.76, p=.4546] or explosions [t(24) = 0.30, p=.7675] indicating that the highly impulsive ADHD group did not have elevated risk taking compared to the CRTL group.
The drug by group interactions were not significant for AAP [F(2,24) = 0.82, p=.3421] or explosions [F(2,24) = 0.55, p=.5865]. There was a significant main effect [F(2,24) = 4.01, p=.0313] of drug on AAP, however neither MEC nor NIC was significantly different from PLC.

### 3.3 Characteristics of High Risk Takers

Given extant evidence for rate dependent effects of nicotine on cognition (Dews, 1977, Perkins, 1999) and the absence of a group difference on risk taking, we re-examined our sample to characterize baseline risk taking. A median split based on baseline risk taking propensity, AAP during first 10 balloons of PLC, was used to create a low risk taking group (LRT) and high risk taking group (HRT).

### 3.5 Behavioral Measures and Side Effects

Both drug conditions were well tolerated and there were no serious adverse events. Mixed model ANOVAs found no significant differences on the Physical Symptom Check List (PSCL) total score, or on physical discomfort items on the subjective visual analog scale (SVA; i.e. physical comfort, headache) or the investigator completed objective visual analog scale (OVA; i.e. sweating, gastrointestinal distress).
Examination of mood related variables found no interaction of drug and group on any measure of the SVA or OVA. There were significant main effects of drug on the alertness [F(2,24) = 10.32, p=.0006] and sense of interest [F(2,24) = 4.79, p=.0127] items of the SVA with NIC associated with greater alertness and interest compared to PLC (Supplemental Table 1 contains full results from SVA and OVA).
On the OVA there were significant main effects of drug on the drowsy [F(2,24) = 19.79, p<.0001] and alertness [F(2,24) = 20.14, p<.0001] subscales. Both MEC and NIC were significantly different from PLC on these items (Supplemental Table 1) with NIC associated with less drowsiness and more alertness while MEC was associated with greater drowsiness and lower alertness scores.

## 4. Discussion

This study found significant effects of single doses of nicotine and mecamylamine on risk taking as measured by the Balloon Analog Risk Task (BART). For individuals with high baseline risk taking propensity nicotine reduced risk taking. For subjects with low baseline risk taking mecamylamine increased risk taking. These findings suggest a broad role for nicotinic receptor functioning in the regulation of risk taking behavior for individuals with both pathological and non-pathological risk taking.

It is interesting that d-amphetamine influenced risk taking in the opposite direction of the nicotine effects reported in the current study. This suggests that the mechanism for the nicotine effect on risk taking is likely different from the mechanism for the effect of d-amphetamine.
Nicotine is known to stimulate the release of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain (Clarke and Pert, 1985, Levin *et al.*, 1990, Rapier *et al.*, 1990) which has led to the suggestion that nicotinic potentiation of dopamine release may be a primary mechanism for many cognitive and behavioral effects of nicotine.
The data from the current study are inconsistent with this notion, and instead fit well with data demonstrating that nicotine and methylphenidate (which blocks the uptake of norepinephrine and dopamine) have separable effects on cognitive function in human and animal models (Potter and Newhouse, 2004, 2008) presumably through separable mechanisms. Methodological differences between the two studies including characteristics of the subjects and the timing of drug dosing may also contribute to the discrepant findings. Future studies directly testing the effects of different neurotransmitter manipulations on risk taking are necessary to address these questions.
The Steinberg 2010 model of risk taking, which proposes that the interaction of impulsive responding and heightened reward sensitivity is related to high levels of risk taking in adolescents, may be useful for understanding the findings from pharmacological studies of BART performance. We propose that in the current study nicotinic acetylcholine receptor function modulates risk taking both by improving impulsive responding (via cholinergic transients in prefrontal cortex) and by influencing reward processing (via dopaminergic modulation of the mesolimbic reward system).
This fits with studies demonstrating that nicotine improves response inhibition in ADHD, an effect that is hypothesized to reflect cholinergic transients related to the occurrence of the stop signal (Potter

### Clinical Implications

The data suggest that there may be a behavioral benefit (regulation of risk taking behavior) gained from self-administration of nicotine in high risk taking individuals. Therefore, targeting nicotinic receptors may be a useful pharmacologic strategy to reduce risk taking behavior in individuals with pathological levels of risk taking. It will be important to move beyond reliance on DSM-IV diagnoses as the sole measure of pathological risk taking as our data and others support a dimensional approach to understanding pharmacological effects on complex behavior such as risk taking.
In addition to implication for treating psychopathology, these data also have implications for smoking cessation. Nicotine withdrawal may increase risk taking behavior leading to poor decision making such as smokers placing themselves in situations where they are likely to relapse to smoking.

…

### Summary

Taken together the results of this study demonstrate that acute manipulation of nicotinic cholinergic receptor function has significant effects on risk taking behavior in the BART. These effects are dependent on baseline levels of risk taking such that for individuals with high baseline risk taking nicotine reduced risk taking behavior and for those with low baseline risk taking mecamylamine increased risk taking behavior.
These findings cannot be explained by global effects of drugs on physical side effects, mood related variables, or arousal. There is a large literature demonstrating baseline dependent effects of nicotine on measures of cognition, behavior, and mood (Dews, 1977, Perkins, 1999), and results from the current study are consistent with this literature.
While the mechanism for these effects on risk taking cannot be fully determined from this study, they are consistent with improved attention and/or impulse control via cholinergic neurotransmission in frontal cortex, likely in combination with regulation of reward processing related to cholinergic modulation of dopaminergic neurotransmission. Finally these results underscore the important distinction between risk taking and impulsivity as subjects who were carefully selected for clinical (ADHD diagnosis) and behavioral (SST performance) indices of impulsivity were not a high risk taking sample.
